findings.title: Remove unverified remote-script execution from Dockerfile
findings.whyItBreaks: The added `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes arbitrary remote code at image build time with no integrity check (no SHA-256 pin, no pinned version/tag, no GPG signature verify). The URL is `example.com`, a reserved placeholder domain (RFC 2606) used only in documentation, so the artifact does not actually exist: `curl -sL` silently follows redirects and suppresses errors, and the pipeline's exit status is that of `sh` (the last command), which succeeds on empty stdin — so the intended install silently no-ops while the image still builds, masking a broken/unavailable dependency. Bundling a `curl | sh` into the base image is a known supply-chain injection surface: any compromise of the host or a future change to the URL silently becomes unverified remote code execution inside the image.

findings.title: curl|sh executes unverified remote code at build
findings.whyItBreaks: The added RUN pipes a remote script straight into 'sh' with no checksum/signature/version pin. '-sL' follows redirects and suppresses errors, so the executed content can be swapped or change between builds (non-reproducible, supply-chain injection surface) with zero verification. Compounding it, the pipe swallows curl's failure: with no pipefail and no 'set -e', a failed/blocked download feeds empty stdin to 'sh' (exit 0), so the RUN 'succeeds' and the image is built WITHOUT the tool that the subsequent COPY app and CMD /app rely on — an undetected silent-install failure. Piping unverified remote content into the image build adds a path that executes arbitrary code on every rebuild.

findings.title: Pipe unverified remote script into sh at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: The added `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads an arbitrary remote script and executes it directly in the shell during image build, running as root, with no integrity verification (no pinned version, no checksum, no signature). The URL is also a placeholder: example.com is a reserved domain that serves an HTML page, so the build either executes unexpected/unverified content or fails non-reproducibly. Because curl is called without `--fail`, a 404/redirect body is still piped into sh rather than failing the build, so a broken or malicious upstream silently becomes the executed payload. This is the canonical remote-code-execution/supply-chain injection vector and makes the image non-reproducible and non-auditable.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing with empty
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for a missing key (src/store.go:10). LoadOrDefault does `v, _ := Load(key, m)` (line 16), discarding that error and returning the empty string. An exported/public path now returns "" for BOTH a missing key AND a key legitimately present with an empty value, so no caller can ever distinguish 'not configured' from 'configured to empty'. Any caller that feeds the result into downstream logic (routing to a host, enabling a flag, building a signature) silently acts on a default it cannot detect as a fallback — precisely the failure-as-value hazard. The name 'LoadOrDefault' also promises a default that isn't parametrized: the fallback is hard-wired to the zero value.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows missing-key error, conflates with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load (line 7) returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and (v, nil) otherwise. LoadOrDefault ignores the error with `v, _ := Load(key, m)` and returns v, so an absent key yields "" exactly like a present key whose stored value is "". Because LoadOrDefault is exported and returns no error or presence flag, every caller is forced to conflate "key missing" with "key present but empty" — a silent loss of the ErrMissing signal that Load exists specifically to expose. Acting on that fallback (e.g. treating an absent config value as an empty-but-valid one, or persisting the empty string) is unsafe.

findings.title: Run returns before results are delivered (no WaitGroup/close)
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces synchronous sends with `go func(j int){ results <- j*2 }(j)` per job. The previous body delivered every `j*2` before `Run` returned. Now `Run` schedules the goroutines and returns immediately, with no `sync.WaitGroup` and no closing of `results`. Consequences on a live caller: (1) a caller that reads `len(jobs)` values from `results` right after `Run(...)` returns may block (unbuffered) or observe fewer/fewer values because the sends are not guaranteed to have started; (2) a caller that follows `Run(...)` with `close(results)` (the idiomatic completion signal) races the still-pending goroutine sends, producing a 'send on closed channel' panic or dropped results; (3) if the caller consumes fewer than `len(jobs)` values, the goroutines leak forever on unbuffered sends. The original ordering (job order) is also now nondeterministic. The closure correctly captures `j` by value, so this is purely a missing-synchronization defect, not a capture bug.

findings.title: Run fires goroutines but loses its completion contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The change wraps each `results <- j * 2` in `go func(j int){...}(j)` and drops any wait, so `Run` returns immediately after spawning goroutines instead of only after all sends complete. This silently flips the exported function's semantics. Two concrete failures: (1) A valid caller pattern that relied on Run having delivered everything — `ch := make(chan int, len(jobs)); worker.Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` — now panics with "send on closed channel", because the goroutines are still sending after Run returns and close(ch) races them. (2) With an unbuffered channel or a buffer smaller than len(jobs), the N goroutines block forever on `results <- j*2` after Run returns, leaking goroutines. `results` is `chan<- int` (send-only), so Run cannot close it to advertise completion either, leaving callers with no way to know when the work is done. The goroutine capture is correct (`j` passed by value), so only the completion-contract regression is the defect.

findings.title: Wait for spawned goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run synchronously delivered every `j*2` value to `results` before returning. Now it launches a goroutine per job and returns immediately, so the function gives no guarantee the sends have completed and provides no completion signal (no sync.WaitGroup, no close(results)). Any caller that relies on the old contract — e.g. `results := make(chan int, len(jobs)); Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` — races the in-flight goroutines against the close and panics with "send on closed channel"; if `results` is unbuffered and no receiver drains it concurrently, the goroutines block forever and leak. Ordering of results is also no longer guaranteed to match `jobs` order, since goroutine scheduling is nondeterministic.

findings.title: AND→OR widens delete authorization, allowing non-admin deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: canDeleteRecord gates record deletion. The original conjunctive check required BOTH fields: an admin and a tenant match. The change to a disjunction (session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId) makes the gate pass when EITHER condition holds. Two concrete privilege escalations follow: (1) any non-admin user whose session.tenantId matches the record's tenantId is now authorized to delete — previously regular users were blocked; (2) any admin (isAdmin=true) is now authorized to delete records in ANY tenant, breaking cross-tenant isolation. Both remove the tenant/admin restriction that the predicate previously enforced, so the function can now authorize an action the old contract never allowed. This is an externally-visible deleted record (data loss) authorized by a weakened gate, not a behavior-neutral refactor.

findings.title: Loosened authorization expands who may delete records
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || weakens the delete gate, which is the security boundary for a destructive operation. Truth table (session.isAdmin, tenantMatch): old returned true only for (true,true) — admin AND same tenant. New returns true for (true,false) — any admin regardless of tenant, enabling cross-tenant record deletion — and for (false,true) — any same-tenant user regardless of admin, giving non-admin tenant members delete rights. Both were previously denied. `record.ownerId` is never consulted, so the same-tenant branch also ignores ownership. This is an authorization bypass / privilege escalation on a destructive path; a strict reviewer cannot merge it without intent evidence and a test.

findings.title: Admin can now delete records in any tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` to `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId` removes the tenant-scope constraint for admins. A session where isAdmin=true no longer needs its tenantId to match the record's tenantId, so an admin of tenant A can delete records owned by tenant B. In a multi-tenant model this is a cross-tenant authorization bypass / privilege escalation and potential cross-tenant data deletion. The change is also a silent widening of a public security API with no accompanying test or justification.

findings.title: Swallowed parse errors wipe valid settings on corrupt input
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, parseSettings threw on invalid JSON or a non-string theme / non-number fontSize, so updateFontSize aborted and never called save(). With a single page of size 10 you can never render the 11th item, so the last item becomes unreachable — silent content loss. The floor result is wrong whenever totalItems is not an exact multiple of pageSize, including the totalItems>0 but <pageSize case (e.g. pageCount(1,3)=0 pages even though one item must be displayed). This is a fresh regression: the base version returned Math.ceil, which is correct for every positive input.

findings.title: buildReport pairs builtFrom with artifacts from a different commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The public BuildReport contract implies builtFrom is the commit whose artifacts are listed (both fields previously came from the same `commit`). After this change, builtFrom = build.ref(branch) while artifacts = build.artifactsAt(build.ref('verified')). Whenever the 'verified' ref resolves to a different commit than `branch`, a caller receives a report whose artifacts did not come from the commit named by builtFrom, so the provenance it advertises is wrong. The asymmetry is the defect: only the artifacts source was switched, leaving builtFrom on the branch ref, so the two fields no longer describe one build. This is an exported function/interface, so the inconsistency is the contract itself, independent of any current in-repo caller.

findings.title: buildReport artifacts no longer match builtFrom ref

The change fetches artifacts from a hardcoded, unrelated ref `build.ref("verified")` while `builtFrom` is still computed from `build.ref(branch)`. Because these are two independent `ref()` calls with different named arguments, the returned BuildReport now contradicts itself: it claims to be built from <branch>'s commit but lists artifacts for a different, magic-string ref. Any caller that trusts `.builtFrom` and then uses `.artifacts` (e.g. to deploy, verify, or publish what it thinks it built) can act on artifacts that do not correspond to the reported build, or get empty/missing artifacts if the "verified" ref does not exist. This is a regression from the previous consistent behavior of an exported public function (the contract itself is now broken regardless of callers).

When the branch ref and the 'verified' ref resolve to different commits, the returned BuildReport pairs the branch's commit label with artifacts that may not belong to that commit. The original code guaranteed builtFrom and artifacts corresponded; this change silently breaks that invariant with no documentation of the new semantics, so a caller displays a report builtFrom=X that lists artifacts from a different commit Y.

findings.title: recentEntries no longer honors limit, returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor removed `slice(0, limit)` from the positive-limit path. When `limit > 0`, the function now `return sorted` (the full reversed array) instead of at most `limit` entries, contradicting its doc comment 'Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first.' The sole caller `renderFeed` (src/feed.ts:9-10) trusts this cap: it allocates `new Array<string>(20)` and copies `page.length` elements. With >20 inputs, `page.length` exceeds 20 and `out[i] = page[i]` grows the array past 20, so `renderFeed` returns more than 20 entries. This is a user-facing regression in the feed's page size.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit — returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaced `return [...all].reverse().slice(0, limit);` with `const sorted = [...all].reverse(); if (limit <= 0) return []; return sorted;`. The `.slice(0, limit)` cap was dropped entirely. For any positive `limit`, the function now returns every entry in `all` instead of at most `limit`, directly violating its own doc comment ('Returns at most `limit` entries'). The in-repo caller `renderFeed` calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and preallocates `new Array<string>(20)`, relying on `page.length <= 20`. With the regression, when `all.length > 20` the loop `for (let i=0; i<page.length; i++) out[i]=page[i]` extends `out` past index 19, so `renderFeed` now returns the full feed rather than a 20-entry page — a user-facing feed-content regression.

findings.title: RecentEntries drops the limit cap for positive limits
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`, so positive `limit` returned at most `limit` entries. The new body replaces the slice with `return sorted;`, so for any `limit > 0` it returns ALL entries, not the cap. This contradicts the doc comment 'Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first.' It is also a live regression: `renderFeed` calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` (line 9) and then writes `out[i] = page[i]` for each `i < page.length` (line 11) into an array primed to size 20 — so the feed now grows to the full entry count and the 20-item page cap is silently gone. The `limit <= 0` guard is unrelated to this and does not cover positive limits.

findings.title: entry-count header ignores stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now renders only live (non-stale) rows via `entries.filter(e => !e.stale)`, but the header still passes the full `entries.length` to headerLines. So the emitted `# entry-count: N` reports the total number of entries including stale ones while the body lists a smaller set of rows. Previously the count always equaled the row count; any consumer that parses `# entry-count` and then iterates/validates that many rows now reads fewer rows than the header claims (mismatch). On an all-non-stale input the behavior is unchanged, so the defect only surfaces exactly when the filter has an effect.

findings.title: entry-count header no longer matches rendered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The change filters stale entries out of `rows` (src/manifest.ts:20-21) but the header count still uses the full `entries.length` (src/manifest.ts:22, `headerLines(opts, entries.length)`). Previously count always equaled the number of rows; now, whenever any entry has `stale === true`, the emitted `# entry-count: N` over-reports the number of rows that follow. Any consumer that parses the manifest by trusting `# entry-count` to know how many rows to read will mis-size the read (index out of range / truncated parse) or fail a count-vs-rows validation. The filter should be reflected in the count.

findings.title: manifest entry-count header now disagrees with row count

Before this PR, `count = entries.length` and the body produced one row per entry, so the header count exactly equaled the number of rows. The change filters the rows to only non-stale entries (`live = entries.filter(e => !e.stale)`) but still passes `entries.length` (the total, including stale entries) to headerLines. When any entry has `stale === true`, the header declares more entries than the body contains. A consumer that reads `# entry-count` and then iterates/validates that many `path\tsize` rows (completeness check, progress, buffer sizing) will see fewer rows than promised, treating a complete manifest as truncated/incomplete. The contract carrier (`# entry-count`) promises the number of listed entries; the body no longer honors it.

This PR keeps `commit: head` (the channel's head) but changes `files` to repo.filesAt(stable), i.e. files from a different ref ("stable"). Whenever the channel head differs from "stable", the returned Snapshot is internally inconsistent: any consumer that pairs `commit` with `files` (e.g. building release artifacts, changelogs, or diffing against the recorded commit) will read file contents that do not belong to the commit it was given. This is silent — no error is raised, so callers trust a snapshot whose files and commit are unrelated. It also adds a new hard dependency: `repo.headCommit("stable")` must resolve, so publishing on a repo without a "stable" ref now throws where it previously succeeded.

For any channel other than "stable" the returned Snapshot claims commit=<channel-head> but its `files` are the tree of the *stable* channel's head — commit and files no longer match. The base version returned `files: repo.filesAt(head)` (files at the same commit it reported). Any consumer that trusts `commit` to describe `files` receives mismatched data, and publishing to a non-stable channel silently produces the wrong file set. This is a regression on the function's core contract (Snapshot = commit + channel + files for that commit).

Any caller that passes a df it still needs afterwards (e.g. building several variants from one shared/source frame, or a df loaded from a global/shared store) silently has that df overwritten by the mapping, even though `apply_values` reads as a pure transformation. findings.title: changeset changedPaths computed against a different revision than fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: fromRevision (line 17) is set to store.resolve(pinnedTag), but changedPaths (line 18) is now computed via store.readChangedPaths(latest) where latest = store.resolve("latest"). As soon as pinnedTag resolves to anything other than 'latest', the two fields diverge: changedPaths lists only paths that changed since latest, so paths changed between the pinned tag and latest are silently dropped, and a consumer that replays the changeset onto fromRevision applies a diff whose base does not match. Files changed between `from` and `latest` are silently omitted, and files changed only between `latest` and the current state are wrongly included, so a consumer replaying the changeset applies an incorrect path set. findings.title: Restore error propagation in Charge instead of swallowing to nil

Any caller that branches on the error will treat a declined/failed charge as successful — persisting the charge, not retrying, or issuing a receipt. findings.title: async await in reserve adds oversell race (lost update)
findings.whyItBreaks: `reserve` now reads `remaining` (line 15), then `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) yields to the event loop, then writes `this.stock.set(...)` (line 18). The base was synchronous so read+write were atomic; the new `await` interleaves two concurrent reservations: both read the same `remaining` (e.g. 1 for the last unit), both call `save(sku, 0)`, both return `true`, and both set memory to 0. Inventory of 1 unit reserves 2 units (oversell / lost update), and the store is told the same failing value twice. A timeout or slow I/O in `save` widens the window.

findings.title: reserve() race can oversell inventory after adding await
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR reserve() was synchronous and atomic (read remaining, guard, set) with no yield point, so within the single-threaded event loop no two calls could interleave. The PR inserts `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) between the `remaining <= 0` guard (line 16) and `this.stock.set(sku, remaining - 1)` (line 18). Two overlapping async reserve calls now both read `remaining = 1` from the same `stock` map, both pass the guard, both await save, then both execute `set(sku, 0)` and both `return true` — the last unit is reserved twice. Result: two consumers are told they hold the last item (over-sell) and the persisted/in-memory stock under-reports availability (lost write). The fix must make the read-guard-decrement a single atomic step (e.g. a queue/lock, or do the decrement synchronously and persist after, or compare-and-set against the stored value after the await).

findings.title: Async reserve() has a non-atomic check-then-act race (oversell)
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version read `remaining`, checked `<= 0`, and set stock all synchronously, so the reserve was atomic in JS's single-threaded loop. This PR inserts `await this.store.save(...)` between the check (line 16) and the in-memory decrement (line 18). `reserve` is now async, so it yields at the await. Two concurrent calls for a SKU with 1 unit both execute the sync prefix: each reads `remaining = 1`, each passes `if (remaining <= 0)`, each suspends at the await, then each persists `save(sku, 0)` and each sets stock to 0 — and both return `true`. That grants two reservations for one available unit (double-sell/lost update). The synchronous version could never interleave, so this is a regression, and inventory reservation is exactly a system that sees concurrent requests for the same SKU.

findings.title: backoff unit change not propagated to retry.ts consumer
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)) and the diff correctly removed the *1000 multiplier in schedulePoll. But src/jobs/retry.ts:12 is unchanged and still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). With the new ms return value, the retry sleep becomes backoff(a)*1000 ms: attempt 0 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min), attempt 1 = 2,000,000 ms (~33 min), attempt 4 = 16,000,000 ms (~4.4 hr), attempt >=5 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 hr). The retry loop effectively hangs for hours per attempt, breaking the retry workflow.

findings.title: backoff unit change makes retry backoff 1000x too long
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)), but the existing caller retry.ts at src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still treats the return value as seconds and computes sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). The *1000 is now double-applied: attempt 0 sleeps 1000*1000 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1s; attempt 5+ sleeps 30,000*1000 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.3h). The retry workflow hangs for hours per attempt. The diff updated only poll.ts (setTimeout(cb, backoff(attempt)), correct for the new ms unit) and left retry.ts on the old seconds contract.

findings.title: retry.ts multiplies backoff() by 1000 after it now returns ms
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt*1000), cap 30s) but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). The *1000 is applied twice, so the retry delay is 1000x too long: attempt 0 -> backoff=1000ms *1000 = 1,000,000ms ~16.7min (was 1s); once capped, backoff=30_000ms *1000 = 30,000,000ms ~8.3h (was 30s). The retry loop effectively hangs for hours on any transient failure, leaving jobs stuck and downstream operations waiting.

findings.title: Swallowed f.Close() error: save can report success on failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaces `return f.Close()` with `defer f.Close()` + `return w.Flush()`. The deferred Close discards its error return. bufio.Writer.Flush() only writes buffered bytes to the *os.File via Write; it does not surface errors that occur at close() time (delayed-write/EIO on network filesystems, disk-full surfacing at close, NFS writeback failures). In the base, those errors reached the caller as the function's return value; now Save returns nil, so a caller (and this is an exported public API) believes the file was durably written when it was not. This is a regression in error reporting on the primary success path.

findings.title: Report f.Close() error instead of deferring it silently
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code ended with `return f.Close()`, so a caller of the exported `Save` received a non-nil error if closing the file failed. The new code replaces that with `defer f.Close()` (line 13) and `return w.Flush()` (line 20); the deferred Close runs after the flush but its error is discarded. On filesystems where a final close/commit can fail even after a successful write (e.g. NFS delayed commit, CIFS, FUSE), `Save` now returns nil — indistinguishable from a genuine success — and a caller that persists/bills on the nil error will treat a non-durable write as saved. This is a silent-error-loss regression on a public persistence contract.

findings.title: Return close error instead of defer f.Close() swallowing it
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `return f.Close()` (the success-path error propagation) and replaces it with `defer f.Close()`, which discards the error return. When `bufio.Writer.Flush()` succeeds writing the buffered bytes into the kernel, the residual disk-commit failure (e.g. ENOSPC on NFS/FUSE, or a late write error reported only at close) was previously surfaced to the caller by `Save`'s error return; now it is silently dropped and `Save` returns nil. Because `Save` is exported, every caller that checks its returned error to decide 'file was durably saved' now conflates a failed close with a legitimately successful save and treats it as success. `defer d.Close()` is a classic unchecked-close pattern that static analyzers (errcheck) and Go's guidance specifically flag on write paths.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of each page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds() returns half-open [start, end) bounds (its own docstring line 18: 'Half-open [start, end)'), so the page's rows are rows[start:end] and the loop must iterate range(start, end). The rewritten loop iterates range(start, end - 1), which stops one short of end and excludes the last row of every page. Substituting real values: rows=['a','b','c'], page_size=10 -> page_count=1, _window_bounds gives start=0, end=3, range(0,2) yields only ['a','b']; summarize() renders '1. a\n2. b' and silently drops '3. c'. For rows length 25 with page_size 10, pages drop indices 9, 19, and 24 (the final row of the whole dataset) — every page loses its last row, and a single-row page yields an empty window (range(0,0)). The docstring 'Rows belonging to page_index' (line 25) promises the full page, so this is also a contract drift where the body implements less than it promises. The base implementation used range(start, end) and returned all rows, so this is a regression, not pre-existing behavior.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of each page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: The new loop `for position in range(start, end - 1):` iterates the half-open interval [start, end-1), so the element at index end-1 (the last row of the page) is never appended. The base code used `range(start, end)`, and `_window_bounds` explicitly promises a half-open [start, end) bound, so this is a regression. Concrete: rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=3 -> page_index=0 returns ['a','b'] instead of ['a','b','c']; page_index=1 returns ['d'] instead of ['d','e']. Because render_page and summarize both call page_window, the final row of every page is silently omitted from the rendered output (data loss in the displayed result), with no error raised.

findings.title: page_window off-by-one drops last row of each page
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code iterated range(start, end); the rewritten loop iterates range(start, end - 1), excluding the final index of every page. Every full page loses its last row, and a trailing partial page (where start == end-1, e.g. a single-row last page) yields an empty window, so its row is never emitted. page_window feeds render_page and summarize, so rendered output silently drops one row per page and can omit the entire final row. Verified: rows=['a','b','c','d'], page_size=2 -> summarize returns '1. a\n---\n3. c' (b and d missing); rows=['a'], page_size=2 -> the only row is never rendered.

findings.title: Invert TTL freshness check in cache get
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from `<` to `>`. Base behavior: fresh entry (age < ttlMs) returns its value; expired entry (age >= ttlMs) is deleted and get returns null. Head behavior is the exact inverse: a fresh entry (age < ttlMs) now fails the `>` test, so it is deleted and get returns null (cache miss on live data), while an expired entry (age > ttlMs) passes and is returned as if valid. The cache never serves fresh data and serves stale expired data indefinitely.

findings.title: pruneDone skips done jobs and mutates input
findings.whyItBreaks: Replaced `jobs.filter(job => !job.done)` with `forEach` + `splice(index, 1)`. Two defects: (1) Mutating an array while iterating with forEach skips the element that shifts into the spliced index, so consecutive done jobs survive. Example `[done, done, notdone]`: index 0 splices, array becomes `[done, notdone]`, forEach advances to index 1 and sees `notdone`, leaving the second `done` — result `[done, notdone]` instead of `[notdone]`. (2) The original returned a fresh array without mutating the caller's; the new code mutates the caller's array in place and returns the same reference, a contract/side-effect regression for any caller that retains the input.

findings.title: TtlCache.get returns expired entries, evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshness comparison was inverted from `<` to `>`. Base behavior: age < ttl -> fresh -> return value; otherwise delete + return null (expired). HEAD behavior: age > ttl -> return value (an EXPIRED/TTL-stale entry now served as valid), and age <= ttl -> delete + return null (a still-FRESH entry is evicted). Age == ttl also evicts. The class is named TtlCache and its set() writes storedAt=Date.now(); the correct contract is 'return while age < ttl, evict after'. This inverted version serves stale data and destroys valid cache hits, defeating the entire cache and risking stale value read as fresh.

findings.title: pruneDone splices inside forEach, skipping consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: splice() during forEach shifts elements but forEach captured the original length once, so an element that slides into the just-deleted index is never re-checked. Example [a.done=false, b.done=true, c.done=true]: index1 removes b -> array becomes [a,c]; forEach advances to index2 which no longer exists (length 2) so c (done) is left in the result. The base filter(!done) removed every done job and returned a NEW array; HEAD mutates the caller's input array in place and returns the same reference (a contract change on a public exported function) and under-removes when >=2 consecutive jobs are done.

findings.title: TTL cache get() inverted: returns expired, evicts fresh
findings.whyItBreaks: The operator was flipped from `<` to `>`. A TTL cache must return the value when the entry is fresh (`Date.now() - storedAt < ttlMs`) and delete it once expired. The new code does the reverse: it returns `entry.value` only when the entry is EXPIRED, and for fresh entries falls through to `this.entries.delete(key)` and returns null. Every call now either serves stale/expired data (a live correctness/security risk) or deletes a still-valid entry, making the cache behave opposite to its contract.

findings.title: pruneDone splices during iteration, skips consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Mutating an array with `splice(index, 1)` inside `forEach` shifts subsequent elements left, so the iteration index skips the element that just moved into the current position. Consecutive `done` jobs are therefore not all removed. Verified: `[{done:true},{done:true}]` returns `[{done:true}]` (the second done job survives) and `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:true}]` returns `[{done:true}]`. Additionally the original `filter` returned a NEW array without touching the input; this version mutates the caller's array in place, so any caller holding the original reference now observes it modified — a contract change on a public function.

findings.title: Restore empty-rows guard so averageAmount returns 0, not NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`. With an empty `rows` array, `reduce` yields `total = 0` and the function now computes `0 / 0 = NaN`. Any consumer (e.g. averaging a day's transactions when none exist, or multiplying the average by a count) receives NaN instead of the prior value 0, and NaN poisons subsequent arithmetic. This is the exact contract the removed guard preserved; no replacement guard was added.

findings.title: busiest must not mutate the caller's rows array
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR changed `[...rows].sort(...)` to `rows.sort(...)`. `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place, so `busiest` now reorders the array the caller passed in. Callers that pass a shared/derived array and later iterate or persist it expecting the original ordering will see it silently reordered — a side-effect change the function signature does not advertise. The base code made a defensive copy and left the caller's data untouched.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty rows (guard removed)
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array guard `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` was removed. For an empty input, `reduce(..., 0)` yields `total=0` while `rows.length===0`, so the function now returns `0 / 0 = NaN` instead of the previous `0`. Empty input was an explicitly handled, legitimate case in the base; NaN silently poisons any downstream average/aggregate arithmetic (e.g. `sum + NaN`, comparisons, formatting) and is indistinguishable from a failed computation. This is a behavior regression on a changed, exported public function.

findings.title: busiest now sorts/mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The defensive copy was dropped: `[...rows].sort(...)` was replaced with `rows.sort(...)`. `Array.prototype.sort` mutates the receiver, so the caller's array is now reordered in place as a side effect of a function whose contract is to return the busiest row. Any caller that still holds `rows` and relies on its order (insertion order, subsequent paging, dedup, or re-display) observes corrupted/reshuffled data. This is a dropped-defensive-copy regression on an exported public function. Verified: after the call the input reference is reordered to descending amount.

findings.title: averageAmount now returns NaN for an empty rows array
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removed the `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard (base line 7). At head, an empty array makes `total = 0` and `rows.length = 0`, so the function returns `0 / 0 === NaN`. NaN is a silent poison value that propagates through any downstream arithmetic/aggregation as a public exported function. This is a regression: the previous behavior for the same input was `0`.

findings.title: busiest mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff changed `[...rows].sort(...)` (base line 13, which copied the array via spread) to `rows.sort(...)`. `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place and returns the same reference, so calling `busiest(rows)` now reorders the caller's own array, permanently mutating its data. Any caller that passes a `rows` array and later relies on its original ordering, or that shares/reuses/persists that array, gets corrupted ordering. This is an unintended in-place mutation of caller data.

findings.title: topPlayers ranks by lexicographic string sort, dropping correct top players
findings.whyItBreaks: rankScores does scores.sort() (default comparator) then .reverse(). Default sort converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically, so a numeric array is not ordered numerically. The descendant cutoff at line 15 is then taken from a mis-ordered array, so topPlayers filters on a wrong threshold and slice(0,n) returns wrong/missing players. Example: [{a,100},{b,10},{c,50}], n=2 → expected [a,c]; actual cutoff=100 → only [a] returned, dropping the 50-point player. The producing line is the changed sort at line 8; the former `(a,b)=>b-a` comparator was removed. formatBoard (line 20) inherits the wrong board.

findings.title: rankScores uses lexicographic sort, breaking top-n ranking
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator coerces elements to strings and sorts lexicographically, not numerically. The base version used scores.sort((a, b) => b - a) (numeric descending). After this change scores are sorted by string value then reversed, so multi-digit scores sort incorrectly. Example: scores [100,10,2,3,5] produce sorted+reversed [5,3,2,100,10]; cutoff = scores[2] = 2, so topPlayers(players,3) filters score>=2 and returns the first 3 in original order (e.g. [100,10,2]) instead of the true top 3 [100,10,5]. The wrong cutoff directly changes the set of players returned, and formatBoard (line 19-23) propagates the same wrong ranking to its output. Verified with node: const a=[10,2,3,100,5,1]; a.sort(); a.reverse() yields [5,3,2,100,10,1], which is not descending.

findings.title: sort() without comparator breaks numeric ranking
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically, NOT numerically. Reversing the result does not yield descending numeric order when scores have differing digit counts. Example: scores [9,10,11], n=2. rankScores -> sort() gives [10,11,9], reverse() gives [9,11,10]; cutoff = scores[1] = 11, so topPlayers filters to score>=11 and returns only [11]. The old sort((a,b)=>b-a) gave [11,10,9], cutoff=10, and returned [11,10]. So topPlayers (and its caller formatBoard) silently drop valid tied/low-ranked players and return the wrong set. This is a user-facing correctness regression in the leaderboard's only exported function; it breaks for any scores whose string representation differs from numeric order (e.g. 9 vs 10 vs 100), which is the common case.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff changes the signature verification from hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) to signature_of(...) == given_signature. Python's str.__eq__ is not constant-time: it returns at the first differing byte, so per-character timing differences leak the secret-derived signature. verify() is the sole authentication gate in handle() (returns 401 on mismatch, else 200 + processor(payload)), so an attacker can recover the HMAC-SHA256 signature byte-by-byte over many requests and forge a valid signature, bypassing webhook authentication and invoking processor(payload) with attacker-controlled input. The entire purpose of compare_digest in HMAC verification is to be timing-safe; removing it is a real security regression (CWE-208), not a style change.

findings.title: Restore constant-time compare for webhook signature check
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) with signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature. The == operator short-circuits at the first mismatching byte, so response timing reveals how many prefix bytes of the expected HMAC-SHA256 signature match. verify() is the sole authentication gate for handle() (app/webhook.py:14), which returns 401 vs 200 and runs processor(payload). An attacker who measures timing across many guesses can recover the expected signature byte-by-byte and forge a valid signature, bypassing the webhook auth boundary. This is a present security regression, not a speculative concern.

findings.title: Avoid non-constant-time signature comparison (timing side-channel)
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the sole authenticity gate for webhook requests (handle() returns 401 and never calls processor when it returns falsy). The diff replaces `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` — a deliberately constant-time comparison that runs in time independent of how many prefix characters match — with the string `==` operator. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits at the first differing byte, so the comparison runtime leaks how many leading characters of the attacker-supplied signature match the true HMAC-SHA256. A remote attacker who can measure response timing can recover the valid signature byte-by-byte (CWE-208) and then forge authenticated calls, gaining access to `processor(payload)`. The previous code explicitly used the constant-time primitive for this exact reason; this diff removes it with no functional benefit, leaving `hmac` still imported and unused by verify.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so they committed or rolled back together. This refactor keeps only `_record_ledger` (the INSERT) inside the transaction, which commits on block exit, and calls `_apply_balances` (the two UPDATEs) OUTSIDE the transaction. Now the ledger record is durably committed before the balance changes run. If the debit UPDATE succeeds but the credit UPDATE fails (e.g. constraint violation, DB error, network), the debit is applied without the corresponding credit and the ledger already records the transfer — funds are silently lost. If the balance updates fail entirely, the ledger shows a transfer that never affected any balance. The two UPDATEs are also no longer atomic with each other, so partial application is possible.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code ran the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so all three committed or rolled back together. The refactor keeps only `_record_ledger(...)` inside the transaction (line 23) and calls `_apply_balances(...)` at line 24 AFTER the `with` block has already committed. Now if `_apply_balances` raises (e.g. the debit UPDATE hits a CHECK constraint for insufficient funds, or the increment fails), the ledger row is already persisted but the account balances are not updated — the ledger records a transfer that never happened in balances. In addition, the two UPDATEs inside `_apply_balances` are no longer atomic with each other: a failure between the decrement and the increment leaves only one side of the balances changed. The transaction no longer guards the money movement it was written to protect.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction, breaking transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: The original code ran the ledger INSERT, the debit UPDATE, and the credit UPDATE all inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so they committed atomically. The refactor pulls `_apply_balances` (the debit and credit UPDATEs) out to line 24, AFTER the `with` block has already committed the ledger INSERT. Now: (1) the ledger row persists even if the subsequent balance updates fail, so the ledger records a transfer that never actually happened; (2) `_apply_balances` itself runs with no transaction, so if the credit UPDATE (balance = balance + cents) fails after the debit UPDATE (balance = balance - cents) succeeds, the source account is debited but the destination is never credited — funds are lost and the accounts table is inconsistent. This is exactly the atomicity guarantee the single transaction existed to provide, and the regression is unconditional (the happy path works only when nothing fails).

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to local timezone, shifting billable day
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate. This change swaps them to getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so billingDay now depends on the runtime process TZ. For any instant whose local date differs from its UTC date (e.g. 2026-01-15T01:00:00Z under America/Los_Angeles is still 2026-01-14 locally), billingDay returns the previous day. The same UTC instant yields different 'billing days' on servers in different timezones, and can roll the day back mid-window relative to the UTC-based contract the original code established. since this is the only exported API of the module, every future caller and sameBillingDay comparisons are affected by server-locale nondeterminism.

findings.title: billingDay regressed from UTC to local-time date computation
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation computed the billing day with the UTC getters (getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate), anchoring billing boundaries to UTC. The new version uses local-time getters (getFullYear/getMonth/getDate). For any runtime whose timezone offset is non-zero and where the local calendar date differs from the UTC date, the same Date instant now yields a different billingDay string. Verified with new Date('2024-01-01T00:30:00Z') under TZ=America/New_York: the UTC version returns '2024-01-01' while the new local-time version returns '2023-12-31'. A billing day that shifts with the server timezone mis-attributes charges/events to the wrong day, breaking date-keyed billing aggregation. This is collateral damage from the pad-helper refactor, not an intentional timezone change; there is no indication a local-time anchor was desired.

findings.title: billingDay changed from UTC to local time, shifting day boundary
findings.whyItBreaks: Base used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; head uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. For any timestamp whose local date differs from its UTC date (i.e. an offset timezone around midnight), billingDay returns a different value than at base. Billing day is typically used to group transactions against a deterministic boundary, so this introduces a timezone-dependent result that varies with the runtime's local TZ (e.g. a server in UTC-5 at 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z yields '2023-12-31' now vs '2024-01-01' at base), which can mis-bucket transactions near the boundary. This is a silent semantics change on a public exported function with no in-repo caller or spec confirming the local-time intent.

findings.title: Memo key omits tenant, returns wrong tenant's profile
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile is tenant-scoped: it takes a `tenant` parameter, calls fetchProfile(tenant, account), and the returned Profile carries a `tenant` field (src/profile.ts:2,10,12,17). The module-level `memo` map is shared across all calls, but the cache key was changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account` (src/profile.ts:14). After readProfile('tenantA', 'acct1') caches a profile, a later readProfile('tenantB', 'acct1') returns tenantA's cached profile instead of fetching tenantB's, silently mis-routing the wrong tenant's data. This is a cross-tenant data leak/wrong-result regression that a single-account key cannot distinguish.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile(tenant, account, fetchProfile) is tenant-scoped: it passes both tenant and account to fetchProfile (line 17), and Profile carries a tenant field (line 2). The memo cache is now keyed only by `account` (line 14). If two tenants share an account identifier, the first lookup (tenant A, acct X) caches its Profile under key "X", and a later lookup for (tenant B, acct X) hits that cache entry and returns tenant A's profile. The returned data no longer corresponds to the requested tenant — a wrong-data regression and a cross-tenant data leak. The base key `${tenant}:${account}` uniquely scoped the entry and is deliberately lost here.

findings.title: Restore tenant in cache key: cross-tenant collision serves wrong profile
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile now memoizes purely on `account`. fetchProfile(tenant, account) is tenant-dependent and the returned Profile embeds `tenant`, so two tenants that happen to use the same account value (common when account numbers are tenant-scoped) collide in `memo`. The second tenant's `readProfile(tenantB, acct1)` returns the first tenant's cached Profile (tenant: 'tenantA'), silently serving the wrong tenant's data to callers that trust the returned Profile.tenant/account.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The added `catch { return ""; }` discards the `missing: ${key}` error (and any other error from `store.get`) and substitutes an empty string. The previous contract of `load` was to throw on a missing key; now a missing key is indistinguishable from a legitimately-stored empty string value. The in-repo caller `loadAll` (src/store.ts:11-13) maps each key through `load`, so a missing key now yields `""` in the array instead of propagating the failure. Any consumer that stores `""` as a real value can no longer detect a missing entry, which is silent error loss: a caller can persist, report, or act on the fallback as if it were real data. The fallback is not part of the API contract, the error is not logged, and failure vs. the empty value is not distinguishable at any decision point. This is an exported/public swallow site, so the contract defect stands regardless of future callers.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error, returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The added `catch { return ""; }` (lines 6-7) converts the `missing: ${key}` throw (line 4) into an empty-string return. `load` is an exported public function, and its sole in-repo consumer `loadAll` (line 12) now silently maps every missing key to '' instead of propagating the error that previously aborted the batch. Because a Map<string,string> may legitimately hold '' as a value, a caller who does `load('k', store)` can no longer distinguish 'k not present' from 'k stored as empty' — and no error is surfaced for a genuinely missing key. This is a swallowed-failure regression relative to the base, where a missing key threw.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error, returns "" conflating absent vs empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported load() previously threw `missing: <key>` when store.get(key) was undefined, letting callers distinguish an absent key from a present one. The new catch-all converts that error (and any other error) into `""`. Because the return type is `string`, a key that legitimately holds an empty string is now indistinguishable from a missing key, and loadAll() silently maps absent keys to `""` instead of surfacing the failure. The explicit throw at line 4 is now dead: it is thrown and immediately caught and collapsed to `""`. Any caller that relied on the thrown error to detect a missing key (e.g. to abort, log, or fall back) now receives a plausible empty value and can no longer tell failure from a real value. findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer so large diffs don't abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` from the `git()` spawnSync call, dropping the cap to Node's default of 1024*1024 (1MB). `git()` is the function that generates the entire review patch (`git diff mergeBase headSha` at line 140) and the changed-file list. When the base branch has advanced past the point the PR branched from (the normal case for a PR opened against a moving main), `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes commits that landed on main between the merge-base and the base tip — commits that are NOT part of this PR. The original code deliberately derived the merge base for exactly this reason (the `merge-base baseSha headSha` call is only meaningful when `baseSha` can differ from the merge base). findings.title: String replace() now expands $ patterns in injected JSON/patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff changes the replacement argument of three String.prototype.replace calls from a function form (`.replace("{{X}}", () => value)`) to a string form (`.replace("{{X}}", value)`). With a function replacement, the returned string is inserted literally; with a string replacement, JavaScript interprets special substitution sequences in it. When JSON.stringify(bundle) (line 25), JSON.stringify(candidate) (line 32), or bundle.patch (line 33) contain `$&`, `$'`, `` $` ``, or `$$`, the injected content is rewritten before being sent to runCodex. I verified directly with node: for the string `"pre{{BUNDLE}}post"`, replacing with `"a$&b$'c$`d$$e"` yields `"prea{{BUNDLE}}bpostcpred$epost"`, whereas the function form preserves the literal `a$&b$'c$`d$$e`. So a patch line like `echo $'...'` or `PID=$$` inside the bundle, or shell/`$&`/`$'` text in findings or agentsMd, gets expanded into the prompt prefix/suffix or `{{BUNDLE}}` literals or a dropped `$`. This silently mangles the review/critic prompt (and can inject the entire surrounding prompt text into the middle of the injected JSON), corrupting the codex input and the resulting review. The base code deliberately used the function form; this is a regression.

The base code used function-form `() => value` precisely so the return value is spliced literally with NO substitution. Head replaces all three calls with the string value itself: line 25 injects `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` directly and line 33 injects the raw `bundle.patch` diff. `bundle` serializes an arbitrary git diff/`repoPath`, so `$&`, `$'`, `` $` ``, or `$$` inside that text is now interpreted as a replacement token. `$'` (text-after-match) duplicates the trailing half of the prompt into the patch placeholder and `$&` splices `{{PATCH}}`/`{{BUNDLE}}` into the prompt; `$$` silently drops a `$`. Result: the review/critic prompt fed to the model is corrupted and the produced review is wrong. This is a regression introduced by this PR (base was safe; head removes the guard).

The largest consumer is `git diff baseSha HEAD` (line 30) whose stdout becomes the entire `patch` fed to review(). The guard `if (res.status !== 0)` is then true (null !== 0), so git() throws `git diff <base> HEAD failed:` and runLocal aborts. PRs with diffs over 1MB (many files, lockfiles, vendored/generated content) previously worked up to 64MB and now fail outright — the same PRs the tool exists to review. Note gh() retained its maxBuffer, so this is not a deliberate global policy change.

findings.title: PR patch and changed-file set derive from different snapshots
findings.whyItBreaks: `patch` is now fetched from GitHub via `gh pr diff` (line 143), which reflects the PR head/base as GitHub computes it. But `changedFiles`/`changedPaths` (lines 144-145) still come from `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` against the local checkout `HEAD` (line 57), and `headSha` is now `pr.head?.sha` (line 140) while the local `HEAD` is left implicitly referring to the merge-ref commit. On a standard `pull_request` Actions checkout, `actions/checkout` sets `HEAD` to the merge commit (`refs/pull/N/merge`), which differs from the PR head `pr.head.sha` and from the base the PR was actually branched from. Whenever the base branch has advanced, the merge contained conflicts, or the checkout ref is not the PR merge ref, the file set named in `gh pr diff` and the file set returned by `git diff baseSha HEAD` diverge. The `changedPaths` set at line 145 is what `inlineComments` (lines 61-70) uses as a filter, so a finding on a file present in the GitHub PR diff but absent from the local `git diff` is silently dropped, and surface classification can disagree with the reviewed patch. In the common clean-merge path they happen to align, so this is an edge-case correctness risk, not a guaranteed break.

findings.title: patch from gh pr diff but changedFiles still from local git diff
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, `patch` and `changedFiles` were BOTH computed from `git diff baseSha HEAD`, so the diff text and the changed-file set were guaranteed to agree. Now `patch` comes from `gh pr diff <prNumber>` (GitHub's three-dot merge-base diff of the PR) while `changedFiles`/`changedPaths` still come from the local `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` (changedFileSet at line 57, consumed at line 145). These two sources diverge whenever the local checkout is not exactly at the PR's head/merge state (e.g. base branch advanced past the PR's merge-base, or a non-merge/head checkout), so `git diff --name-only <base tip> HEAD` can list files changed on the base branch that are NOT in the `gh pr diff` being reviewed. `inlineComments` (line 63) gates comment placement on `changedPaths.has(f.file)`, so a finding on such a file would post an inline comment on a path/line that is not in the PR diff; GitHub rejects the review POST and `postReview`'s catch (lines 96-110) silently falls back to a body/event-only review, dropping all inline comments. The reviewed diff and the gate that decides where comments are placed are no longer derived from one source.

findings.title: Self-review bypass: PR controls the tool that reviews it
findings.whyItBreaks: The old 'trusted-tool pattern' checked out the reviewer from frankekn/needlefish@main (trusted) into a separate dir and ran it against the PR head checkout at path 'target'. Its own comment said this 'prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool.' The change deletes that trusted checkout, checks out the PR head SHA at the repo root (line 43-47), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against the PR head's lockfile (line 51), and executes the PR head's own `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 59) with GH_TOKEN granted `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` (permissions block, lines 16-19). Any PR to this repo that modifies src/cli.ts (or the lockfile, or any file the tool imports) now controls the tool that reviews it: it can emit a PASS/approval for its own PR, write false check runs / review results, or read the repo contents via the token — i.e. the review gate becomes self-defeating. The same-repo `if` guard (line 24) narrows the attacker to someone with push access, but that is exactly the population the review gate is meant to police, so the trust boundary removal is a real regression.

findings.title: Restore severity case/whitespace normalization and P1 fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` does a strict, case-sensitive match, but the prior `String(raw.severity ?? '').trim().toUpperCase()` coercion was removed. A lowercase or whitespace-padded severity that used to normalize correctly (e.g. raw `'p2'` → `'P2'`, raw `' P0 '` → `'P0'`) now fails the includes() check and falls through to the default. The default was also lowered from `'P1'` to `'P3'`. Net effect: a real `p2` finding is silently down-classified to `P3`, and any missing/invalid severity now defaults to `P3` instead of `P1`. This corrupts the severity field of every normalized finding for non-canonical input, changing downstream prioritization/classification of the review output. Note the associated `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? '').trim().toUpperCase();` line was deleted. Category normalization (`category` block) still coerces properly, but severity no longer does.

findings.title: Restore severity case normalization to avoid P1->P3 downgrade
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and now tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)`. SEVERITIES = ["P0","P1","P2","P3"] (line 85) contains only uppercase values, so any severity input in a non-exact-uppercase form (e.g. "p1", "P1 ", "critical") fails the membership check and falls through to the fallback, which this PR also changes from "P1" to "P3". A legitimate "p1" finding is thus silently reclassified as P3. Because `normalizeReview` maps every raw finding through `normalizeFinding` (line 132) and the function is exported, the public normalized `Finding.severity` contract now conflates a real severity with the minor fallback — downgrading findings that should be triaged as serious. Previously the normalization handled arbitrary case/whitespace; its removal is a behavior regression on the exported normalization path.

findings.title: Restore severity case/whitespace normalization; lowercase P0 now becomes P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` normalization and passes `raw.severity` straight into the SEVERITIES membership check. SEVERITIES is `["P0","P1","P2","P3"]` (all uppercase). Because `normalizeFinding` is fed LLM review output via `normalizeReview(raw: any)` (free-form text), values like `"p0"` or `"P0 "` are NOT in SEVERITIES, so they now fall through to the default `"P3"` instead of normalizing to `"P0"`. This silently downgrades a genuinely critical finding to the lowest severity — de-prioritizing and potentially unblocking a real P0 security bug — and the fallback default was also lowered from `"P1"` to `"P3"`, so missing/invalid severity is now treated as least-severe.

findings.title: Restore token stripping before codex subprocess spawn
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the block that built a sanitized env ({...process.env} minus GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN) and passes it to spawnSync. With the env option removed, spawnSync falls back to inheriting the full parent process.env, so GitHub credentials now flow into the `codex` agent subprocess. codex is an LLM-driven agent (run with `-s read-only`, which only sandboxes filesystem writes, not env reads) that can read its environment via shell/env tools and reflect those values in its `--output-last-message`, which runCodex reads back and returns. This is a regression of an intentional credential-isolation control, exposing repo CI credentials to an untrusted subprocess.

findings.title: Restore stripping of GitHub tokens from codex subprocess env
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff deletes the only sanitization that removed GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawning the codex CLI. spawnSync with no `env` option defaults to the full `process.env`, so those credentials are now passed to the child process. codex runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath` — the repository being reviewed, which is untrusted input — and executes tools/commands in that repo. Any command codex runs (or that the review prompt induces it to run) inherits the complete environment, including the user's GitHub credentials, creating a token-exfiltration path that the original code explicitly guarded against.

findings.title: Restore env sanitization before spawning codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch deletes both the sanitized `env` construction and the `env,` option passed to spawnSync. Node's spawnSync inherits process.env when no env is specified, so the codex child process now receives the full parent environment, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. These credentials were deliberately stripped before this diff; restoring the default env hands GitHub auth tokens to an AI agent subprocess (CODEX_BIN is configurable, and the agent runs tooling and emits output that is captured and returned). read-only sandboxing limits filesystem writes, not the child's ability to read its own environment, so the stripping was a real control and its removal is a security regression with no functional benefit.

findings.title: Restore fork-PR guard; fork code runs on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing keeping fork PRs off this job. It is gone, so every `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened) from a fork now triggers the workflow. The job runs on `runs-on: self-hosted`, checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (the fork's code), then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (package lifecycle scripts are attacker-controlled via package.json) and executes `tsx src/cli.ts` — i.e. arbitrary attacker code runs on a persistent self-hosted machine. Even though GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only and other secrets are not passed on fork `pull_request` events, the runner itself is exposed to RCE and whatever credentials/network it holds. This is a supply-chain/security bypass introduced solely by this deletion.

findings.title: Fork protection removed: fork PRs now run untrusted code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only check that stopped PRs from forks. `pull_request` (types: opened/synchronize/reopened) fires for fork PRs by default, so any external user can open a fork PR and have this job run. The job runs on `runs-on: self-hosted`, checks out the attacker-controlled `head.sha` (actions/checkout@v4, ref: ${{ ...head.sha }}), then executes `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` — which runs attacker-supplied package.json/lockfile `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall` scripts — and then runs the attacker-controlled review CLI via `tsx src/cli.ts` on that same self-hosted machine. This is arbitrary code execution on the maintainer's runner infrastructure from an unauthenticated fork PR, plus the head checkout supplies untrusted source/dependencies that the workflow itself executes. The removed line was exactly the defensive control for this shape; nothing else in the repo replaces it (rg finds no other fork guard). This is a supply-chain/security bypass on a privileged runner.

findings.title: Removing fork guard allows RCE on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only gate excluding fork PRs. With it gone, any fork PR to this repo triggers the `review` job on `runs-on: self-hosted`. The job then checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (the fork's untrusted commit), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (fork-controlled lockfile/package.json can run install scripts), and executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (the fork's source). This is arbitrary code execution from an untrusted fork on a trusted, self-hosted runner — a supply-chain/RCE exposure. Note the `permissions` block (contents: read, pull-requests: write, checks: write) does not mitigate this: for the `pull_request` event from a fork the GITHUB_TOKEN stays read-only, but the fork code still executes before any token use and the runner host itself is the attack surface. The guard was effective: for a fork PR, `head.repo.full_name` (e.g. attacker/needlefish) != `github.repository`, so it correctly skipped fork PRs; same-repo branch PRs still passed.

findings.title: Env var set to 0 now silently falls back to default
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`, so a configured value of `0` in NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS is now rejected and replaced with the default (5000 / 2000). `0` is a legitimate, meaningful setting for these timers: it expresses 'no grace period / no give-up wait'. Concretely, an operator who sets NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 to force an immediate SIGKILL right at the timeout now gets a 5000ms grace instead, so a runner that ignores SIGTERM keeps running 5s past the configured `invocation.timeoutMs` before being killed (line 124 setTimeout reads RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS). Likewise NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now waits the default 2000ms (line 123). An explicitly-set `0` is silently ignored rather than honored, changing timeout semantics on upgrade.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so changed files are never silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed block (base lines 98-110) guaranteed every changed file got deep-reviewed by pushing any file not in a selected hotspot into a 'tail-coverage' hotspot. Now `hotspots` is only `sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (head line 93) with no backstop. On a large PR, the map pass can return more than MAX_HOTSPOTS (6) hotspots, and any changed file that lands in a hotspot ranked below the top 6, or that is not assigned to any surface, is never deep-reviewed at all — the exact 'never silently skip a changed file' guarantee the comment documented is now reversed. Bugs in those files can pass un-reviewed.

findings.title: Do not abort entire large review on one hotspot failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code wrapped each deep pass in try/catch (base lines 122-129): a failure was recorded as a `blocks: true` residual risk and the loop kept going, so findings and checked entries from the other hotspots were preserved and still returned. Now `normalizeReview(extractJson(runCodex(...)))` is called bare (head line 103): a single transient deep-pass failure (model/network/malformed JSON) throws out of `reviewLarge` with no result, discarding `all` and `checked` accumulated from every earlier hotspot. A large-PR review therefore fails entirely on one bad hotspot instead of returning partial findings plus a blocking residual — a robustness regression that makes the tool fragile to a single transient error.

findings.title: Drop deep-review residual risks; blocks signal lost
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep pass returns RawReview whose residual_risks[] may carry a blocks:true flag ('could not verify X, would block'). The loop now does `all = all.concat(res.findings)` and drops `res.residual_risks`, and candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded to []. Those per-hotspot signals previously flowed into the critic's {{FINDINGS}} context and from there into pruned.residual_risks -> deriveVerdict. Now they never reach it, so a deep pass that reported an unresolved blocking risk cannot block the final verdict: the review can return PASS (blocks:false) while a deep reviewer flagged a deferred/blocking risk. This is a swallowed failure signal (TRIGGER D) with no compensating log or passthrough.

findings.title: One hotspot failure now aborts entire large review
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch was removed. Previously a throw from runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview for a single hotspot was caught, recorded a blocks:true residual plus a 'DEEP PASS FAILED' checked[] entry, and the loop continued to review the remaining hotspots, still returning a ReviewResult. Now any single deep-pass failure propagates out of reviewLarge -> review() and throws, so the whole review returns no ReviewResult at all: no partial findings, no diagnostic, and a transient API/parse error in one hotspot crashes the pipeline instead of degrading to a blocked-but-complete review. This also removes the only observability of which hotspot failed (the checked[] 'DEEP PASS FAILED' entry).

findings.title: Coverage backstop removed; changed files may be skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The tail-coverage backstop (which appended a hotspot for every changed file not present in the selected hotspots, with an explicit comment 'never silently skip a changed file') was deleted. In the large path the hotspot list is now only `sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`. Any changed file the map pass fails to assign to a surface — or that falls outside MAX_HOTSPOTS — is no longer deep-reviewed and is silently skipped, reintroducing exactly the silent-skip case the removed rule guarded against. This only bites when the map pass under-covers, so severity is limited.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop so changed files are never silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed block added a 'tail-coverage' hotspot for any changed file not present in the selected hotspots, and its comment stated the purpose: 'never silently skip a changed file.' With only `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (cap 6) remaining, a changed file that map.md assigns to a hotspot ranked below the top 6, or to no surface at all, is never deep-reviewed. For a large PR (the whole point of reviewLarge) this silently drops those files from review, so a real defect in an unmapped/low-rank file goes undetected.

findings.title: Per-hotspot deep-review failure now aborts the whole large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: The try/catch around each deep review was removed. Previously a throw from runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview in one hotspot was caught, logged as 'DEEP PASS FAILED' in `checked`, and recorded as a `blocks:true` residual risk so the review continued and returned a partial result. Now any single hotspot failure propagates out of reviewLarge and out of the exported `review()`, discarding the already-completed map pass and any prior hotspot results and returning no ReviewResult at all. A transient LLM failure in one hotspot thus takes down the entire large-PR review.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual risks before the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is hardcoded to `[]`, replacing the former `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` accumulation. Each deep review's own residual risks (including `blocks:true` uncertainty) used to reach the critic via `JSON.stringify(candidateMerged)` at line 116; now the critic receives an empty array and cannot surface or propagate that blocking uncertainty into the final `pruned.residual_risks`, so the verdict derived by `deriveVerdict` can come back clean even when a deep pass flagged unresolvable concerns.

findings.title: large-PR path drops focus/deep inputs that small-PR path still honors
findings.whyItBreaks: The public Bundle contract still carries `focus` and `deep` (the diff does not change the type), and `reviewSmall` still passes the whole bundle into review.md via `{{BUNDLE}}`, so a caller's focus directive and deep flag ARE honored on the small path. On the large path, `reviewLarge` now builds `mapBundle` without `focus`/`deep` (lines 84-89) and no longer substitutes `{{FOCUS}}` in the deep prompt (line 117-121). Result: the same `review()` call, given the same `focus`/`deep`, produces a focused/deep review for small patches but silently ignores both for large patches. The user's intent is dropped with no error or warning (silent loss of an input), and the map pass no longer knows whether deep mode is on, so it cannot adjust its blast-radius survey accordingly. This is a behavior regression vs. the base, where both fields were threaded into the map and deep prompts.

findings.title: Removed {{FOCUS}} replace leaves literal placeholder in deep prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code ran .replace("{{FOCUS}}", () => bundle.focus ?? "(none)") on the deep.md template, which is only meaningful if deep.md contains the {{FOCUS}} token. This PR deletes that replacement line but the diff touches only review.ts (deep.md is unchanged), so at HEAD deep.md still contains {{FOCUS}} and it is now passed to the model literally, unsubstituted. The large-PR deep pass also loses the user's focus hint entirely (bundle.focus/bundle.deep are no longer read anywhere in reviewLarge). An unreplaced template token in the deep prompt degrades the review and can make extractJson/normalizeReview throw, which pushes a blocks:true residual and skips deep coverage for that hotspot.

findings.title: formatDuration emits 'Nm 60s' when seconds round to 60
findings.whyItBreaks: The minutes and seconds components are now computed independently: minutes is floored from ms, while seconds is rounded from the sub-minute remainder. When that remainder is >= 59500ms, Math.round((ms % 60000)/1000) yields 60, but minutes is not incremented. For ms in [119500, 119999] the function returns '1m 60s' (and '2m 60s' for [179500,179999], etc.) instead of the correct '2m 0s'/'3m 0s'. This is a regression from the previous implementation, which rounded total seconds first (Math.round(ms/1000)) and then derived minutes and seconds via floor and modulo, correctly rolling the overflow into minutes. Both call sites in renderMarkdown (per-call stats at line 75 and total duration at line 80) render these strings, so a single long model call (>= ~2 minutes) produces a visibly malformed duration in the review output. Verified: 119500 -> old '2m 0s', new '1m 60s'; 179500 -> old '3m 0s', new '2m 60s'.

findings.title: formatDuration emits "Nm 60s" for durations near minute boundary
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from raw ms (Math.floor(ms/60000)) while seconds are computed from a separately rounded remainder (Math.round((ms % 60000)/1000)). When the sub-minute remainder rounds up to 60 (any ms where ms % 60000 >= 59500), seconds becomes 60 but is never carried into minutes, so the renderer prints impossible durations such as "1m 60s" (ms=119500→"1m 60s") and "2m 60s" (ms=179900→"2m 60s"). The previous code derived both minutes and remainder seconds from the single rounded total (Math.round(ms/1000)), which correctly produced "2m 0s" and "3m 0s". This is a user-facing regression in the per-call and total duration strings emitted in renderMarkdown (stats line). Also for inputs just under a minute (e.g. ms=59999) it now shows "60s" instead of the previous "1m 0s".

findings.title: formatDuration can render 'Xm 60s' due to uncarried rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes with floor(ms/60000) and seconds with round((ms%60000)/1000) independently. When the fractional part of a minute rounds up, seconds becomes 60 but minutes is not incremented. For ms=119999 (1:59.999): minutes=floor(1.99998)=1 and seconds=round(59.999)=60, so the rendered stats string is '1m 60s' — an invalid duration shown to users at render.ts:75 and render.ts:80. For ms=59999 it renders '60s' instead of '1m 0s'. The previous code rounded total seconds first (totalSeconds=round(ms/1000), then minutes=floor(totalSeconds/60), seconds=totalSeconds%60), so minutes and seconds always stayed consistent; this PR removed that carry.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0 despite promising positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The change from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes the parser return 0 for input '0' instead of throwing. This contradicts the exported function's name `parsePositiveInteger` and its own error message `${label} requires a positive integer`, both of which promise strictly >0. A caller passing '0' now silently receives the value 0 (validation relaxed) rather than the contract's rejection, so the function no longer implements the contract its name/message advertise. If 0 is not a legitimate value in the intended domain (e.g. attempts, retries, port), this lets an invalid value through; if 0 is legitimate, the name and error message are now wrong and must be updated.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, contradicting positive contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns 0 instead of throwing. The exported function's name (`parsePositiveInteger`) and its unchanged error message (`${label} requires a positive integer`) both promise that a strictly positive (>0) value is required, but the body now accepts zero. A caller passing "0" silently receives a 0 value that the function claims to reject, so the public contract (name + error text) no longer matches the implementation. Per the public-carrier rule, this is a P2 even with no in-repo caller yet: the promised validation affects the value a consumer receives. If zero is intentionally a legal value (e.g. a 'no timeout' sentinel), the function and its message must be renamed/updated; as-is, the contract is inconsistent and future callers will be misled.
